hints: Focus on what a catalyst actually changes, the activation energy barrier, not the energy of the particles themselves.
Remember the Boltzmann curve itself does not shift with a catalyst, but the activation energy mark moves to the left to a lower value.
Think about what a lower barrier means for success, many more lower energy particles can now react without any heating.
walkthrough:
**Recall the job of a catalyst**

A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, $E_a$. It does not heat the mixture or give particles extra energy.

$$E_a(\text{catalysed}) < E_a(\text{uncatalysed})$$

**Picture this on the Boltzmann distribution**

The Boltzmann curve shows number of particles against energy. The shape and peak stay exactly the same when a catalyst is added, because temperature is unchanged.

Only the $E_a$ line moves left. So the area to the right of $E_a$, the fraction of successful particles, gets much bigger.

**Link to successful collisions**

For a collision to succeed, particle energy must be $\ge E_a$. With a lower $E_a$, particles that were previously too low in energy can now collide successfully. That is exactly the effect described in the correct statement.

options.A: Correct. Lowering $E_a$ means the minimum energy needed for success is reduced, so lower energy particles that would have bounced apart can now react. The Boltzmann distribution is unchanged but many more particles lie beyond the new, lower $E_a$ mark.
options.B: Incorrect. A catalyst does not give particles more energy or create more high energy particles. That is what increasing temperature does. This option confuses lowering $E_a$ with shifting the distribution to the right.
options.C: Incorrect. The number of particles with the most probable energy, the peak of the curve, depends only on temperature and total particles. A catalyst leaves the curve shape and peak height unchanged, it only moves the $E_a$ marker.
options.D: Incorrect. The value of the most probable energy, the peak position on the energy axis, depends only on temperature. A catalyst does not change temperature, so the peak stays in the same place. This again confuses a catalyst with heating.
